text: Every control so far in this course has been about deciding who and what gets to reach a resource — verified identity, compliant devices, micro-segmented networks, assume-breach containment. All necessary, none of it sufficient, because the moment a request is legitimately granted, the data itself has no memory of that decision. Once a file is downloaded, it carries no trace of the access control that released it. Data-centric security is what protects it from that point forward.

Three controls make that possible. Classification means applying a sensitivity label — confidential, internal, restricted — that's machine-readable, so a mail gateway, a cloud app, or a DLP engine can actually act on it, not just display it to a human. Encryption binds the decryption key to a policy rather than a storage location, so the file stays protected wherever it ends up. And DLP inspects the content itself and enforces that same policy consistently, no matter which channel it's moving through.

Here's what that looks like for a highly restricted file: the label marks it, encryption is rights-managed rather than just at-rest, and the decrypt condition checks verified identity, device compliance, and managed location — evaluated at the moment someone tries to open it, whether that's on a corporate laptop or a personal one. That's the real shift: encryption that enforces access control even after the file has left the storage account you control.

DLP only works if it's watching every door the data could walk through, not just one. The same sensitivity policy has to apply to an endpoint file copy onto a USB drive, an email attachment, a browser upload into a cloud app, and even printing. A program that only inspects the email gateway while leaving endpoint copies unwatched isn't protecting the asset — it's locking one door and leaving the window wide open.

Classification, policy-bound encryption, and channel-wide DLP are what let protection travel with the asset instead of stopping at a boundary. Next lesson turns the same never-trust, always-verify thinking toward machine-to-machine traffic — zero trust for APIs and service-to-service calls, where the thing authenticating on the other end of the connection is another service, not a person.
